1:2.t: Colossae was a town in the Lycus valley of Asia Minor, near Laodicea and Hierapolis (4:13).

1:7.t: Epaphras probably founded the church at Colossae.

1:14.t: "Through His blood": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts do not have these words.

2:2.t: "Both of the Father and of Christ": the KJV's reading; manuscripts differ here, many reading "the mystery of God, namely Christ".

2:11.t: "Your whole self ruled by the flesh": the KJV's "the body of the sins of the flesh"; many early manuscripts read "the body of the flesh".

3:11.t: Scythians were nomads from north of the Black Sea, regarded by Greeks as the most uncivilized of barbarians.

4:9.t: Onesimus was the slave of Philemon; see the letter to Philemon.

4:10.t: "Mark, the cousin of Barnabas": the KJV's "Marcus, sister's son to Barnabas"; Greek anepsios, cousin. See Acts 15:37-39.

4:14.t: Luke wrote the Gospel of Luke and Acts. Demas later deserted Paul (2 Timothy 4:10).

4:15.t: "Nymphas ... his house": the KJV's reading; many early manuscripts read "Nympha and the church in her house".

4:16.t: The letter from Laodicea has not survived, unless it is the letter we know as Ephesians.

1:15.t: "Firstborn over all creation" (Greek prototokos pases ktiseos): the KJV's "the firstborn of every creature". "Firstborn" here means first in rank and heir, as the next verse shows: all things were created in Him. It does not mean He was the first created being (compare Psalm 89:27).

1:16.t: "In Him ... through Him ... for Him ... in Him all things hold together": Christ is the agent, goal and sustainer of all creation (compare John 1:3, Hebrews 1:3).

1:19.t: "Fullness" (Greek pleroma): "all the fullness of the Deity lives in bodily form". "Deity" (Greek theotes): the KJV's "Godhead", the divine nature itself, not merely divine qualities. Some false teachers apparently taught that God's fullness was spread among many spiritual beings; Paul says it is all in Christ.

2:9.t: "Fullness" (Greek pleroma): "all the fullness of the Deity lives in bodily form". "Deity" (Greek theotes): the KJV's "Godhead", the divine nature itself, not merely divine qualities. Some false teachers apparently taught that God's fullness was spread among many spiritual beings; Paul says it is all in Christ.

1:24.t: "What is still lacking in regard to Christ's afflictions": not that Christ's atoning work was incomplete, but that Christ's body, the church, must still suffer, and Paul gladly shares in those sufferings.

2:8.t: "Elemental spiritual forces" (Greek stoicheia): the KJV's "rudiments". The word can mean basic principles (the ABCs), the physical elements, or spiritual powers thought to rule the world. See Galatians 4:3.

2:20.t: "Elemental spiritual forces" (Greek stoicheia): the KJV's "rudiments". The word can mean basic principles (the ABCs), the physical elements, or spiritual powers thought to rule the world. See Galatians 4:3.

2:14.t: "The charge of our legal indebtedness" (Greek cheirographon): the KJV's "handwriting of ordinances", a handwritten certificate of debt, an IOU. God canceled it by nailing it to the cross, as a list of charges was posted above the crucified.

2:15.t: "Disarmed" (Greek apekdysamenos): the KJV's "having spoiled", stripped. "Triumphing": the picture is a Roman victory parade, in which captives were led behind the conqueror; see 2 Corinthians 2:14.

2:17.t: "Shadow ... reality" (Greek skia ... soma): the KJV's "a shadow ... the body". The Old Testament festivals were shadows cast by Christ, the substance.

3:14.t: "Love" (Greek agape): the KJV's "charity", from the Latin caritas, which in 1611 meant self-giving love. Agape is not mainly a feeling but committed goodwill that seeks another's good, even an enemy's. See 1 Corinthians 13:1.
